name: Landing beaches, Licata
text: The westernmost Allied landing. Major General Lucian Truscott's US 3rd Infantry Division came ashore on beaches either side of Licata at dawn on 10 July and took the town and its small harbour on the first day, which quickly became a supply port for Seventh Army. A short stop sets the scale of the whole 150-kilometre invasion front.
look: Walk the harbour mole and look at the beaches to east and west. Optional if time is short: Gela is 35 km east on the SS115.
plan: Free, public seafront. Drive to Gela 35 km, about 40 min.

name: Gela seafront and pier, Gela
text: Heart of the American landings. The Rangers attacked the town directly while the 1st Infantry Division landed on the beaches to the east. Over the next two days Italian and German tanks came close to throwing the Americans back into the sea here; only naval gunfire and artillery landed on the beach saved the beachhead.
look: The modern pier on the site of the one blown in 1943, the long beaches to the east, and the old town on its ridge that the Rangers cleared street by street.
plan: Free, public seafront. Parking along the lungomare.

name: Piano Lupo crossroads, near Gela
text: The road junction the 505th paratroopers were meant to seize on the night of 9–10 July. A small group under Captain Edwin Sayre took the complex of Italian pillboxes here and, joined by 1st Division infantry, held it against the German armoured thrust of 11 July.
look: Look for surviving Italian pillboxes on the slope of the Niscemi road and look south over the Gela plain where the German tanks were stopped.
plan: Roadside; pillboxes are on private farmland, view from the road. Busy junction: park with care.

name: 82nd Airborne memorial, Ponte Dirillo
text: The main American memorial to the Sicily campaign, beside the SS115 where it crosses the Acate (Dirillo) river. It lists paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne killed nearby; Biazza Ridge, where Gavin stopped the Tigers, is about three kilometres east. A ceremony is held here every July.
look: The memorial tablet, the restored Italian bunkers of the Ponte Dirillo strongpoint, and the view east to Biazza Ridge.
plan: Free, open access by the SS115. Next: about 100 km (1 h 40 min) east to the Pachino peninsula.

name: Bark West beach, Maucini
text: Where the 1st Canadian Infantry Division began Canada's part in the Italian campaign. The beach is almost unchanged: low dunes, shallow water and the offshore sandbars that grounded some landing craft. Royal Marine Commandos landed on the western sector, and the first Canadian steps on Italian soil were taken here.
look: Walk the sand, find the Canadian flag, and look west along the Roger and Sugar sectors of the landing beach.
plan: Free, open beach; reached by minor roads from Pachino. Can be busy in summer.

name: Operation Husky monument, Pachino
text: A modern monument in front of the town hall recalls the landings on the beaches south and east of Pachino by the Canadians, the 51st Highland Division and other units of Eighth Army. A quick stop on the way north to Syracuse.
look: The monument and its inscription in the town square; coffee in the square before the drive north.
plan: Free, town centre. Syracuse is 55 km, about 50 min.

name: Syracuse War Cemetery, Syracuse
text: About 1,060 Commonwealth soldiers lie here, most killed in the landings and the first days ashore, including many glider-borne men of Operation Ladbroke. British, Indian, South African, Canadian and other graves show how multinational Eighth Army was, and how young most of the dead were.
look: The Cross of Sacrifice, the headstones of the glider pilots and airlanding soldiers, and the rows of Indian graves.
plan: Free. CWGC cemetery, normally open daylight hours; check before you go.

name: Ponte Grande, Syracuse
text: The objective of the first large British glider operation of the war. A few dozen men held this bridge for most of 10 July until the last fifteen unwounded defenders surrendered at 15:30, less than an hour before the relief force arrived and retook it intact.
look: The bridge over the Anapo, the canal ditches, and the view towards Syracuse, the prize the bridge protected.
plan: Roadside on the SS115 at the south edge of Syracuse; park nearby with care.

name: Primosole Bridge, Simeto river
text: Scene of the battle between British and German paratroopers on 13–16 July. Holding this bridge meant opening the road to Catania; losing it cost Montgomery three weeks on the plain beyond. The fighting set British 'Red Devils' against German Fallschirmjäger in one of the first clashes between rival paratroops.
look: The bridge on the SS114, the river banks where the paratroops dug in, and the memorials beside the road.
plan: Roadside on a busy highway; park only where safe. 55 km from Syracuse, about 45 min.

name: Catania War Cemetery, Catania
text: About 2,135 Commonwealth soldiers are buried here, many killed at Primosole and in the fighting for the Catania plain; it holds most of the fallen paratroopers of 1st Parachute Brigade, as well as Highlanders and Durham men who fought for the Gerbini airfields and the Simeto crossings.
look: The paratroopers' and Durham Light Infantry graves, and the view of Etna above the plain that Eighth Army could not cross for three weeks.
plan: Free. CWGC cemetery at Stradale Passo del Fico, west of Catania airport; check hours before you go.

name: Museo Storico dello Sbarco in Sicilia 1943, Catania
text: Sicily's main museum of the 1943 campaign, in the converted sulphur works of Le Ciminiere. It tells the story from Allied, Axis and civilian points of view with uniforms, weapons, reconstructed scenes and a large display of Phil Stern's war photographs.
look: The reconstructed air-raid shelter and Sicilian village square, the uniforms and weapons, and the Phil Stern photo gallery.
plan: Daily 09:00–19:00, last entry 18:00. Adults €8, reduced €4 (prices from 15 April 2026). Check before you go.

name: German War Cemetery, Motta Sant'Anastasia
text: The German war cemetery for Sicily: 4,561 dead, 451 of them unidentified, in a walled vault building at the foot of Etna. Among them is Luz Long, the long jumper who befriended Jesse Owens at the 1936 Olympics. Most of the dead were very young.
look: The five raised courtyards, four of them named after Sicilian provinces, the comrades' grave in the first courtyard and the bronze figure of a dying youth.
plan: Free. Apr–Sep 08:00–18:00; Mar, Oct, Nov 08:00–17:00; Dec–Feb 09:00–16:00 (Volksbund). Check before you go.

name: Centuripe, Enna
text: The 38th (Irish) Brigade of the British 78th Division stormed this cliff-top town on 2–3 August against German paratroopers. Its fall cracked the German Etna line and helped decide Kesselring and Hube to plan the evacuation of the island. Montgomery is reported to have said he doubted any other division in his army could have done it.
look: The view from the town over the Simeto and Salso valleys to Etna and Adrano; imagine the Irish battalions climbing the slopes below.
plan: Free, town centre. Steep narrow streets; park at the edge of town.

name: Agira Canadian War Cemetery, Agira
text: Sicily's only Canadian war cemetery, where the Canadian dead of the island were gathered: 490 Canadians killed in Sicily lie on a hilltop above Lake Pozzillo, looking across to Agira and Etna. It has been a place of pilgrimage for Canadians since 1943, and walkers who retrace the division's route end here.
look: The terraced rows, the views to Agira town and Etna, and the visitors' book full of Canadian messages.
plan: Free. CWGC cemetery on the SS121 east of Agira; check hours before you go.

name: Robert Capa Photography Museum, Troina
text: Troina was the scene of the hardest American battle in Sicily. The museum in the Palazzo Pretura shows 62 prints by Robert Capa, who photographed the fighting and the ruined town. Walk to the upper town for views of the battlefield hills.
look: Capa's pictures of soldiers and civilians, then the views west and south from the upper town towards the hills the 1st Division attacked.
plan: Tue–Sun 10:00–13:00 and 16:30–19:30, closed Monday. Adults €5 (reported). Check before you go.

name: San Fratello ridge, San Fratello
text: From 3 to 8 August the German 29th Panzergrenadier Division held the US 3rd Division on this ridge above the Furiano river. Frontal attacks failed with heavy loss until the Americans took Hill 673 and landed behind the line at Sant'Agata.
look: The flat-topped Monte San Fratello and the Furiano valley below; the town sits on the ridge the Germans held.
plan: Free, town viewpoints. Reached on the SS289 across the Nebrodi from Cesarò, about 1 hr 10 min.

name: Landing beach, Sant'Agata di Militello
text: Patton's first amphibious 'end run' landed Bernard's 2nd Battalion, 30th Infantry, here at 03:15 on 8 August. They achieved surprise, but most of the Germans had already pulled back from the San Fratello line. Patton ordered a second landing at Brolo three days later.
look: The beach west of the Rosmarino river mouth and the coast road the landing force cut.
plan: Free, public beach and seafront.

name: Monte Cipolla, Brolo
text: The second 'end run'. Bernard's battalion landed at Brolo on 11 August and held Monte Cipolla for a day against the 29th Panzergrenadier Division, losing 177 men, before the rest of the 3rd Division broke through the Naso ridge to relieve them.
look: The hill above the coast road between the Naso and Brolo rivers, and the beach below where the landing craft came in.
plan: View from the coast road and Brolo seafront; the hill is farmland. Messina is 85 km, about 1 hr on the A20.

name: Sacrario di Cristo Re, Messina
text: Italy's military shrine for Messina holds the remains of some 1,288 Italian soldiers of the Second World War and 110 of the First. Its terrace gives the best view of the city Patton entered on 17 August and of the Strait across which the Axis escaped.
look: The crypt, the great bell cast from captured First World War guns that rings at sunset, and the view over the harbour.
plan: Free. Opening of the church and crypt varies; the terrace is usually accessible. Check before you go.

name: Capo Peloro, Torre Faro
text: The narrowest point of the Strait, about three kilometres across. The German ferry routes ran from the beaches between here and Messina; the flak batteries around the Strait kept Allied aircraft at bay. This is the best place to understand why the Axis escape succeeded.
look: The lighthouse point and the Calabrian shore opposite; the tall pylon is a relic of a 1950s power line, not the war.
plan: Free, public seafront. Camping Il Peloritano at Rodia is 15 km west.

name: Baytown landing shore, Gallico–Catona (Reggio Calabria)
text: Right beside the ferry port, this stretch of shore north of Reggio is where Eighth Army returned to the European mainland on 3 September 1943, the first Allied landing on the Italian peninsula. It was almost unopposed, which made it a strange beginning for a campaign that would last another twenty months.
look: Walk to the waterline and look across the strait to Sicily, only a few kilometres away.
plan: Free, open shore · 10–15 min from the Villa San Giovanni ferry terminal · then about 4 h 30 min to Paestum

name: US 36th Division monument, Paestum beach
text: The 36th 'Texas' Division came ashore here at 03:30 on 9 September 1943, straight into fire from the 16th Panzer Division. Sergeant James Logan won the Medal of Honor near here that morning, knocking out German machine-gun posts. The memorial by the shore is the best place to understand the American landings at Salerno.
look: Read the monument, walk the sand towards the Torre di Paestum, and look inland across the flat plain to the temples and Monte Soprano.
plan: Free, open access · beach parking along Via Poseidonia (paid in summer)

name: Temples and museum of Paestum
text: The three great Greek temples were on the edge of the 36th Division's beachhead. Both sides treated them as off limits, and Allied medics set up aid stations nearby. Walking among 2,500-year-old columns where shells were landing in 1943 is one of the most striking contrasts of the whole trip.
look: See the Temple of Neptune and the Basilica, then the museum's painted Tomb of the Diver. Look west to the landing beaches 1 km away.
plan: Daily 08:30–19:30, last entry 18:30 · €15 (Mar–Nov), €10 (Dec–Feb), reductions for young visitors · check before you go

name: Altavilla Silentina and Hill 424
text: The hilltop village that dominated the American sector changed hands three times in a week. From here German observers could see every beach and road on the plain, which is why the 36th Division fought so hard for the village and Hill 424 behind it, and why the village itself was shelled from sea and land.
look: Drive up to the old centre and find a viewpoint west over the Sele plain to the sea and the landing beaches.
plan: Free · narrow streets, park below the centre · 25 min from Paestum

name: Sele–Calore corridor, near Ponte Barizzo
text: On the afternoon of 13 September German armour drove down this corridor between the two rivers towards the beaches, and the Allied beachhead came close to being split in two. American field artillery stopped the attack near the Calore. There is little to mark the spot, but seeing how flat and open the ground is explains the crisis.
look: Stop safely on a farm road near the Calore bridge and look north-east up the corridor towards Persano and Altavilla.
plan: No facilities · private farmland: stay on public roads

name: Salerno War Cemetery, Bivio Pratole (Montecorvino Pugliano)
text: The Commonwealth war cemetery for the Salerno landings holds 1,851 graves, 109 of them unidentified, most of them men of the British X Corps who fought between the Sele and Salerno. It lies close to the old Montecorvino airfield and the Battipaglia battlefield. The American dead of Salerno were later moved to the US cemetery at Nettuno.
look: Walk the rows and note the regimental badges of X Corps; the register box by the entrance lists the burials.
plan: Open access (CWGC) · on the SS18 between Battipaglia and Pontecagnano · parking at the gate

name: Museo dello Sbarco e Salerno Capitale, Salerno
text: A volunteer-run museum of about 200 objects covering the landings and Salerno's months as seat of the Italian government (February–July 1944). Outside stand a Sherman tank, a jeep and a sealed railway wagon of the kind used to deport Italian Jews, a reminder that the war in Italy was also a racial persecution.
look: Uniforms and weapons of all three armies, photographs of the beachhead and the story of the 'Salerno capital'.
plan: Visits by reservation only (info@salerno1943-1944.com) · Via Generale Clark, Salerno · check before you go

name: Monument to the Four Days of Naples, Piazza della Repubblica
text: Naples was the first large Italian city to rise against the German occupiers. This monument on the seafront at Mergellina honours the Four Days of 27–30 September 1943 and all who fought, from soldiers to street boys like Gennaro Capuozzo, killed aged 11 or 12 (sources differ).
look: Walk round the four carved panels, then look along the bay: the port the Germans wrecked is to the east.
plan: Free, open · heavy traffic: park and walk, or take the metro to Mergellina

name: Galleria Borbonica air-raid shelter, Naples
text: Naples was one of the most heavily bombed cities in Italy: about 200 Allied raids between 1940 and 1944, with civilian deaths estimated at 20,000–25,000. This 19th-century royal tunnel and old cisterns became a shelter for thousands of people. Graffiti, beds and wrecked cars left here after the war make the civilian experience very real.
look: Guided tour through the shelter rooms, wartime graffiti and the vehicles dumped here after 1945.
plan: Fri–Sun 10:00–17:30, guided tours only, booking required · €11–16 depending on route · entrance Vico del Grottone 4 · check before you go

name: Naples War Cemetery, Miano
text: The main Commonwealth cemetery of Naples holds 1,202 Second World War burials, many of them men who died in the three general hospitals set up in the city after its liberation, as well as soldiers moved in from small burial grounds nearby. It is a quiet counterpoint to the chaos of the city centre.
look: Look for the variety of regiments and nations; the cemetery reflects the whole Allied base in Naples.
plan: Open access (CWGC) · Via Vincenzo Ianfolla, off Corso Secondigliano

name: Royal Palace of Caserta (Reggia)
text: The vast Bourbon palace became an Allied headquarters in the autumn of 1943, first for the US Fifth Army and later for Allied Force Headquarters. Here, on 29 April 1945, German envoys signed the surrender of German and Italian Fascist forces in Italy, which took effect on 2 May. The campaign you are following ended in these rooms.
look: The royal apartments, the grand staircase and the long park with its cascade; imagine offices, map rooms and soldiers' rest camps in the grounds.
plan: Closed Tuesdays · Apr–Sep apartments 08:30–19:15 (last entry 18:15) · €18 full ticket · check before you go

name: Caserta War Cemetery
text: A walled section of the town cemetery holds 768 Commonwealth burials: men who died in the 2nd General Hospital, which worked here from December 1943 to September 1945, prisoners of war who died in the prisoner-of-war hospital at Caserta, and soldiers killed in the Volturno fighting of October 1943.
look: A small, peaceful plot inside the town cemetery; note the Volturno dates of October 1943 on many headstones.
plan: Open during town-cemetery hours · short drive from the palace

name: Volturno crossing, Capua–Triflisco
text: The first great river obstacle north of Naples. On the night of 12–13 October 1943 Fifth Army attacked across the flooded Volturno; here, between Capua and the Triflisco gap, the US 3rd and British 56th Divisions made their attempts. Seeing the steep banks explains why the crossing was so hard.
look: Stop by the river at Capua or near Triflisco and look north to the ridges the Germans held.
plan: Free · roadside stop · Capua's historic centre is worth a short walk

name: Italian military shrine and museum, Mignano Monte Lungo
text: The resting place of 974 Italian soldiers, most of them men of the co-belligerent army that fought beside the Allies after the armistice. Their first battle was here, on Monte Lungo, on 8 December 1943: a failure with heavy losses, followed by success on 16 December. The small museum across the road displays weapons and vehicles.
look: Climb the terraced shrine for the view of Monte Lungo and the Mignano gap; then cross the Via Casilina to the museum.
plan: On the SS6 Via Casilina · museum free, hours vary · check before you go

name: San Pietro Infine: ruined village and Parco della Memoria Storica
text: One of the most powerful war sites in Italy: a whole village left as it was destroyed in December 1943 when the US 36th Division fought for it. The museum in an old olive mill uses sound, darkness and John Huston's film footage to tell the story of the battle and the villagers who sheltered in caves.
look: Walk up through the roofless houses to the church, see the cave shelters, then the museum in Piazza Risorgimento.
plan: Museum Sat–Sun 10:00–12:30 and 14:30–17:00 (summer 16:30–19:00), weekdays on request, booking required · ruins open · check before you go

name: Sangro River War Cemetery, Torino di Sangro
text: The largest Commonwealth cemetery on the Adriatic front, with 2,617 burials from the Sangro battles of November–December 1943 and the winter that followed. British, New Zealand, Indian and other soldiers lie here, and the Sangro River Cremation Memorial names more than 500 Indian servicemen cremated according to their faith.
look: See the cremation memorial and the New Zealand and Indian headstones; the ridge the Germans held rises to the north-west.
plan: Open access (CWGC) · Contrada Sentinelle, Torino di Sangro · about 4.5 km from the Val di Sangro exit of the A14 via the SS16

name: Moro River Canadian War Cemetery, San Donato
text: The heart of any Canadian visit to Italy. Of its 1,615 graves, 1,375 are Canadian, most from the December 1943 battles for the Moro, the Gully and Ortona. It stands on high ground between the river and the town, above the sea, close to where the fighting happened.
look: Walk the terraces of maple-leaf headstones; look north to Ortona and south to the Moro valley.
plan: Open access (CWGC) · Strada San Donato, south of Ortona

name: Casa Berardi, Contrada Alboreto (Ortona)
text: The farmhouse where Captain Paul Triquet of the Royal 22e Régiment earned the Victoria Cross on 14 December 1943, holding on with a handful of men against German counter-attacks. It is a private house, now with holiday apartments, and a memorial recalls the Van Doos' fight.
look: From the road, look at the house and the open fields between it and the Gully to the south-east.
plan: Private property · view from the road unless the owners invite you in

name: Ortona old town and MUBA battle museum
text: Canada's most famous battle in Italy was fought in these streets for eight days at Christmas 1943. Walking from the southern edge of town along the Corso to the cathedral follows the Canadian advance. The MUBA museum tells the story of both soldiers and the 1,314 civilians who died.
look: Corso Vittorio Emanuele, the rebuilt cathedral of San Tommaso and the Aragonese castle above the sea.
plan: MUBA (Corso Garibaldi, Complesso Sant'Anna) is temporarily closed for renovation, no reopening date given · check before you go

name: Santa Maria di Costantinopoli, Ortona
text: In this damaged church on 25 December 1943 the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada held their Christmas dinner in the middle of the battle, companies coming back from the line in turns while the fighting went on a few hundred metres away. The dinner became one of Canada's best-known war stories.
look: The medieval church on Via Don Bosco, south of the old centre, with its 14th-century portal; much of the rest was rebuilt after the war.
plan: Usually closed except for services · view from outside

name: Minturno War Cemetery, Marina di Minturno
text: More than 2,000 Commonwealth soldiers lie here, most of them killed in the crossing of the Garigliano in January 1944 and in the fighting for the hills beyond. It is the natural first stop on the Gustav Line: quiet, beautifully kept and only a few hundred metres from the river they crossed.
look: Read the regimental badges: London Scottish, Royal Scots Fusiliers, North Staffords, Hampshires and many more of X Corps. Note the ages.
plan: CWGC cemetery, normally open daily (CWGC sites in Italy may be locked outside gardeners' hours). On the Via Appia (SS7) near the Garigliano bridge; small car park.

name: Garigliano crossing and Real Ferdinando bridge, Minturno
text: This is where the Via Appia crosses the Garigliano, the western anchor of the Gustav Line. The Germans blew up the 1832 iron suspension bridge in autumn 1943; British engineers bridged the river under fire in January 1944. Beside it lie the Roman ruins of Minturnae, so ancient and modern war sit side by side.
look: Look at the width and current of the river, then north to Minturno on its hill. Combine with the archaeological area if open.
plan: The bridge (restored 1998) is visible from the Via Appia; the Minturnae archaeological area has its own tickets and hours. Check before you go.

name: Museo Linea Gustav, Castelforte
text: A small volunteer-run museum in a town that was almost wiped out. The British 56th Division fought at its gates in January 1944, and the French took it in May. The collection tells the story of the Garigliano front from the viewpoint of the civilians who lived through it.
look: Weapons, equipment and photographs found locally; ask about the fighting for Monte Damiano and the civilian toll.
plan: Via Armando Diaz, in the old centre. Visits by arrangement with the Associazione Linea Gustav Fronte Garigliano (+39 328 681 0710). Check before you go.

name: Monte Maio and the Aurunci mountains, near Ausonia
text: The French breakthrough of 13–16 May 1944 happened in these mountains, which the Germans thought too rugged for a major attack. It unlocked the whole Gustav Line. The villages along this road, among them Ausonia and Esperia, also suffered the worst of the Marocchinate in the days that followed.
look: Stop on the road between Castelforte and Ausonia and look up at Monte Maio, the 940 m summit to the north-east.
plan: Roadside stop only; the summit is a long hike for experienced walkers.

name: 36th Division memorials and the Rapido, Sant'Angelo in Theodice
text: The most painful American site of the campaign. On this bluff the Germans watched the Texas Division try to cross the river below on 20–22 January 1944. Memorials to the 36th Division and a peace bell stand on the edge of the village square, looking down on the crossing sites.
look: Look over the parapet at the Gari (Rapido) below and the flat fields beyond; then turn round to see how Monte Cassino dominates everything.
plan: Piazza G. Mazzini, used as a car park. About 6 km south of Cassino.

name: French Military Cemetery, Venafro
text: The largest French war cemetery in Italy, with the graves of between about 3,400 and over 5,000 soldiers (sources differ, partly because graves from Naples were moved here in 1990–91) of the French Expeditionary Corps, many of them Moroccans, Algerians and Tunisians buried beneath headstones marked for their faith. A detour for those who want to see all the nations who fought for Cassino.
look: Compare the Christian crosses with the Muslim headstones, and read the North African regiments named on them.
plan: About 30 km east of Cassino on the SS85; allow 35 min each way. Extra for long trips. Check before you go.

name: Abbey of Monte Cassino
text: Founded by Saint Benedict around 529, destroyed on 15 February 1944 and rebuilt 'where it was, as it was', the abbey is the reason Cassino is famous. Its bombing remains the most argued-over act of the Italian campaign. Today it is again a working monastery, with a museum and wide views over the battlefield.
look: Look at photographs of the ruins inside, the rebuilt basilica and the view from the terrace down to the town and the Liri valley.
plan: Daily 09:30–18:30 (Apr–Oct), shorter in winter; museum Sundays and holidays only in winter. Modest dress required; paid parking. Check before you go.

name: Polish War Cemetery and Memorial Museum, Monte Cassino
text: More than 1,000 soldiers of General Anders' Polish II Corps lie in this amphitheatre-shaped cemetery facing the abbey; Anders himself was buried among them in 1970. Many of these men had come to Italy via Soviet camps and the Middle East, and could never go home to a free Poland.
look: Read the inscriptions at the entrance and on the terraces, find Anders' grave, then see the museum's films and battlefield relics.
plan: Cemetery on the Strada Albaneta, below the abbey; museum at the entrance. Check before you go.

name: Point 593 memorial, Monte Cassino
text: The white cross on Point 593 marks the summit that the US 34th Division, the 4th Indian Division and finally the Poles fought over from January to May 1944. It is the best place to understand the killing ground of the Cassino massif: rocks, thin soil and no cover.
look: Walk up from the cemetery; on top, find the abbey to the east, Albaneta farm and the Snakeshead ridge to the north-west.
plan: Short, steep, stony path (10–15 min up); good shoes needed.

name: Rocca Janula (Castle Hill), Cassino
text: This medieval castle above the town was taken by New Zealanders on 15 March 1944 and held by the 1/4th Essex Regiment and others against fierce counter-attacks. Restored and reopened in 2015, it gives the classic view of the town battle and of Hangman's Hill below the abbey.
look: Look for the memorial to the 4th Essex; from the walls trace the zigzag road up to the abbey and the rubble zone of 1944.
plan: Reached from Via Montecassino; small entry fee (reported €3). Check before you go.

name: Historiale museum, Cassino
text: Opened in 2004 for the battle's 60th anniversary, the Historiale is Cassino's own multimedia museum, with rooms designed by the Oscar-winning effects artist Carlo Rambaldi. It explains the Gustav Line, the bombing and what the town's 20,000 inhabitants endured, a story easily lost among the military cemeteries.
look: Follow the guided route through the war rooms, the bombing and the postwar rebuilding of a town that had been completely destroyed.
plan: Via San Marco 23. Weekday guided visits at set times; published hours vary between official sources. Check before you go.

name: Cassino War Cemetery and Memorial
text: The largest Commonwealth cemetery in Italy: 4,271 graves, with the Cassino Memorial naming more than 4,000 soldiers of the Italian campaign who have no known grave. British, New Zealand, Indian, Canadian, South African and Gurkha soldiers lie together below the mountain they fought for.
look: Walk the memorial panels by regiment, then look up: the abbey is framed above the headstones.
plan: CWGC. Open during gardeners' hours: about 08:00–12:00 and 13:00–15:30 in winter, 07:30–12:00 and 13:00–16:00 in summer; lock your car. Via S. Angelo, about 1 km from Cassino railway station.

name: German War Cemetery, Caira
text: About 20,000 German soldiers who died in southern Italy lie on the terraced slope of Colle Marino, gathered here from many field graves in 1959–60. The paratroopers who held Cassino are among them. It is a sober counterpart to the Allied cemeteries in the valley.
look: Climb to the bronze cross at the top for a view back down the Rapido valley to Cassino and the abbey.
plan: Via Colle Marino, 3 km north of Cassino. Managed by the Volksbund. Summer Mon–Fri 09:00–18:00, weekends and holidays 09:00–19:00; winter daily 08:00–16:00. Check before you go.

name: Piana delle Orme museum, near Latina
text: A huge private museum of 20th-century life in the Pontine plain, with large pavilions on the Second World War: dioramas of the Anzio landing and Cassino, and a big collection of vehicles. Good for families and vehicle enthusiasts, though less focused than the museums at Anzio.
look: See the Anzio landing pavilion with the Rangers battle and civilian shelters, and the vehicle halls.
plan: Strada Migliara 43½, Borgo Faiti (Latina). Mar–Oct weekdays 09:00–17:00, weekends and holidays to 19:00; Nov–Feb 09:00–16:00 (weekends to 18:00); adult €13. Skip on a short trip. Check before you go.

name: Rangers memorial, Isola Bella near Cisterna
text: A roadside marker and a 'Via dei Rangers' sign recall the destruction of two US Ranger battalions on 30 January 1944. Cisterna itself held out until the breakout of May, when the US 3rd Division finally took the ruined town on 25 May.
look: Look at the flat, ditch-crossed fields and imagine them in daylight with German armour on the road.
plan: On the Via Nettuno about 6 km from Borgo Montello; roadside parking only.

name: Aprilia ('the Factory') and the Via Anziate
text: The centre of the February fighting. Aprilia was a Fascist new town founded in 1936; its tower and buildings became the German strongpoint called 'the Factory'. From here the German attacks of February rolled south down the Via Anziate towards the sea.
look: Stand in the main square, then drive south on the Via Anziate past Carroceto and Campo di Carne, the heart of the defensive battle.
plan: Aprilia is a busy modern town; park near the centre.

name: Beach Head War Cemetery, Anzio
text: 2,316 Commonwealth soldiers lie here, most killed in the defensive battles of February and March 1944 along the Via Anziate. Most are British, with Canadians, South Africans, Australians, Indians and New Zealanders among them. It lies on the road the Germans were trying to reach.
look: Walk the rows of the Guards, the London regiments and the Scots; look north-east towards Aprilia, only a few kilometres away.
plan: CWGC, open access. Via Nettunense, about 5 km north of Anzio.

name: Anzio War Cemetery
text: A smaller Commonwealth cemetery of 1,056 graves on the edge of Anzio, begun just after the landings. Many here were killed in the first weeks: the landing, the advance on Campoleone and the fighting round the Factory. It is often quieter than the larger Beach Head cemetery.
look: Note the dates in late January and February 1944, and the regiments of the British 1st Division and the commandos.
plan: CWGC, open access. About 1 km north of Anzio town off the SS207, near the communal cemetery.

name: Museo dello Sbarco di Anzio (Villa Adele)
text: The town's landing museum, opened for the 50th anniversary, with American, British, German and Italian sections: uniforms, weapons, documents, maps and objects raised from the sea, including from the British cruiser HMS Spartan and destroyer HMS Janus, both sunk off the beachhead.
look: Look for the relief maps of the beachhead and the finds from the sunken ships; then walk down to the harbour.
plan: Via di Villa Adele 2, near the station. Free. The museum's own site gives 10:00–13:00 and 16:00–18:00 (17:00–19:00 in July–August), closed Mondays and Wednesdays; the town's page differs. Check before you go.

name: Museo dello Sbarco Alleato, Forte Sangallo, Nettuno
text: Inside a Renaissance fort built in 1501 on the Nettuno seafront, this museum of the Allied landing displays uniforms, helmets, documents, photographs and material found around Anzio and Nettuno. The fort itself watched the landing ships arrive on 22 January 1944.
look: See the period photographs of Nettuno under shellfire, then look out to sea from the fort.
plan: Via Antonio Gramsci 5, Nettuno. Free. Check before you go.

name: Sicily–Rome American Cemetery and Memorial, Nettuno
text: 7,858 Americans lie here, killed from Sicily to just north of Rome, with 3,095 names of the missing on the chapel walls. The site is on ground captured by the US 3rd Division on 22 January. Its visitor centre and map room explain the whole campaign clearly.
look: Walk under the pines to the memorial; see the bronze relief map and fresco maps of the Italian campaign in the map room.
plan: ABMC cemeteries are normally open daily 09:00–17:00 except 25 Dec and 1 Jan. Free. Check before you go.

name: Mausoleo delle Fosse Ardeatine, Rome
text: Italy's national memorial to the 335 victims of 24 March 1944, opened in 1949 on the site of the massacre. It is one of the most powerful memorials of the war anywhere: the caves, a museum, and a shrine where every victim has his own tomb.
look: Walk through the tunnels, see the small museum, and stand among the 335 tombs, many with photographs and names of the victims.
plan: Via Ardeatina 174. Free. Mon–Fri 08:15–15:30, Sat–Sun 08:15–16:30; museum closes 15 min earlier; closed 1 Jan, Easter Sunday, 1 May, 15 Aug and 25 Dec. Buses 118 and 218; parking at entrance. Check before you go.

name: Museo storico della Liberazione, Via Tasso
text: The building where Herbert Kappler's security police imprisoned and tortured some 2,000 people during the occupation, among them many of the Fosse Ardeatine victims. The cells are preserved with the prisoners' messages scratched on the walls, and the museum is the best place in Rome to understand the occupation.
look: Read the graffiti in the cells, and the sections on the Resistance and the persecution of Rome's Jews.
plan: Via Tasso 145, near Manzoni–Museo della Liberazione metro. Free; the museum's website gives daily 09:00–19:00, closed around Christmas, New Year, Easter and 14–16 August. Check before you go.

name: Porta San Paolo, Rome
text: On 10 September 1943, two days after the armistice, Italian soldiers and armed civilians fought German troops at this Roman gate in a last attempt to keep them out of the city. It is remembered as the first act of the Roman Resistance, and plaques on the walls honour those who fell.
look: Find the memorial plaques on the gate and the Aurelian Walls; the Pyramid of Cestius stands next to it.
plan: Piramide metro (Line B). Combine with the Rome War Cemetery a few minutes away on foot.

name: Rome War Cemetery, Testaccio
text: A small, walled Commonwealth cemetery of 426 graves, used mainly for the garrison after the liberation, with some soldiers and airmen who died as prisoners in Rome. It sits in a quiet corner of Testaccio beside the Protestant Cemetery and a short walk from Porta San Paolo.
look: Note the airmen and the prisoners of war; the Protestant Cemetery next door holds Keats and Shelley.
plan: CWGC. Via Nicola Zabaglia 50, near Piramide metro. For security it is locked outside gardeners' hours (Mon–Fri about 08:00–15:00). Check before you go.

name: Portico d'Ottavia and the Jewish Ghetto
text: Before dawn on 16 October 1943 German police rounded up 1,259 people in Rome, most of them here in the old Ghetto; 1,023 were deported to Auschwitz, and only 16 came back. The square outside the Roman portico is now Largo 16 Ottobre 1943.
look: Look for the memorial plaques and the brass Stolpersteine (stones of remembrance) set into the pavements outside victims' homes.
plan: On foot in the historic centre; respectful dress near the synagogue.

name: Piazza del Campidoglio, Rome
text: On 5 June 1944, the morning after American troops entered Rome, General Mark Clark held his famous press conference on the Capitoline Hill. For a day Rome was the world's headline, until the Normandy landings on 6 June pushed Italy off the front pages, where it largely stayed.
look: Stand at the top of the Cordonata staircase and look over the city that was liberated almost undamaged.
plan: Open square; the Capitoline Museums are separate and ticketed.

name: Via Rasella, Rome
text: Here on 23 March 1944 partisans of the GAP set off a bomb hidden in a rubbish cart as a column of the German police regiment 'Bozen' marched past. Thirty-three policemen and several civilians died. The attack led directly to the Fosse Ardeatine massacre the next day.
look: Walk up the steep, narrow street near the Quattro Fontane crossroads; the attack took place outside Palazzo Tittoni.
plan: Near Barberini metro (Line A). A residential street: please be discreet.

name: Trasimene Line viewpoint, Castiglione del Lago
text: In late June 1944 the lake's western shore was the German Trasimene Line. Castiglione del Lago, on its promontory, is the natural viewpoint over the ridges where British, South African and Canadian troops fought through villages such as Sanfatucchio. It is a short drive from the A1 and a good first stop coming north from Rome.
look: Walk the town walls for the view south over the lake shore; then drive a few kilometres south to Sanfatucchio to see how its houses dominate the road.
plan: Town and lakeside free; the castle and palace museum are ticketed, with seasonal hours — check before you go.

name: Arezzo War Cemetery, Indicatore
text: Arezzo was defended hard in early July 1944 and taken on 16 July by the British 6th Armoured and 2nd New Zealand Divisions. The cemetery holds 1,266 Commonwealth burials from the advance up the upper Arno; plots VII to IX contain the graves of soldiers of the 4th and 8th Indian Divisions, a reminder of how many Indian troops fought in Tuscany.
look: Compare the headstones of the Indian plots, with their varied scripts and religious emblems, with the British and New Zealand rows.
plan: CWGC site at Località Indicatore Zona Prima, north-west of Arezzo; open access, free.

name: Florence War Cemetery, Girone
text: In the Arno valley just east of the city, this cemetery holds 1,632 Commonwealth burials, most of them men killed between July and September 1944 in the approach to Florence and the fighting on the Arno line. The site was chosen in November 1944 for burials from nearby hospitals; 83 graves were later moved here from the Arrow Route cemetery.
look: Look for the regimental badges of British, South African, New Zealand and Indian units carved on the headstones.
plan: CWGC site on the main road at Girone, 2 km towards Pontassieve from the Firenze Sud ring road; bus A14 from Santa Maria Novella to the Girone terminus. Free; the gates are locked outside working hours (roughly 07:30/08:00 to 15:30/16:00 with a lunch break), with a code lock — check before you go.

name: Ponte Vecchio and the demolished quarter, Florence
text: The only Florentine bridge the Germans did not blow on the night of 3–4 August 1944. Popular memory credits Hitler; historians note the Germans chose instead to block it by demolishing the medieval streets at both ends. Today's shops and flats along Por Santa Maria, Borgo San Jacopo and Via Guicciardini are post-war reconstructions on the rubble line.
look: From the bridge, look downstream to Ponte Santa Trinita, rebuilt in 1958 from stones raised from the Arno; the head of its Primavera statue was found in 1961.
plan: Always open; very crowded from late morning, so come early or at dusk. Pedestrian zone: park at a peripheral car park or use the tram.

name: Palazzo Vecchio and Piazza della Signoria, Florence
text: On 11 August 1944, as the Germans withdrew north of the city, the ringing of the Martinella bell in the Palazzo Vecchio tower signalled the rising of Florence's partisans and the Tuscan liberation committee. Fighting went on in the northern suburbs for weeks, with snipers, shelling and more than 600 civilians killed during the battle for the city.
look: Look up at the tower whose bell called the rising, then walk three minutes to the river: for a week German rearguards and Allied troops faced each other across the Arno.
plan: Square always open; Palazzo Vecchio museum ticketed, hours vary by season — check before you go.

name: Florence American Cemetery, Tavarnuzze
text: The only American Second World War cemetery north of Rome holds 4,402 US dead, most of them killed after Rome fell, in the Gothic Line battles and the final push to the Alps. The Tablets of the Missing list 1,409 names. Many men of the 85th, 88th and 91st Divisions who fell at Il Giogo, today's next stop, lie here.
look: Walk the curved terraces up to the memorial; inside, the operations maps trace the campaign from Rome to the Alps.
plan: Via Cassia, Tavarnuzze (Impruneta), 12 km south of Florence; A1 exit Firenze Impruneta. Daily 09:00–17:00, closed 25 Dec and 1 Jan; free — check before you go.

name: MuGot — Museo Gotica Toscana, Ponzalla
text: A volunteer-run museum founded in 2019 between the Futa and Giogo passes, telling the story of the 1944 battles in the Mugello through documents, filmed testimonies, uniforms and recovered equipment. Its guides also lead visits to the battlefields and bunkers of the Gothic Line, so it is the best place to get oriented before climbing to the passes.
look: Ask about the battlefield tour to Monte Altuzzo, and look at the maps of the German positions around the two passes.
plan: Via Ponzalla 47, Scarperia e San Piero. Wed and Fri 09:30–13:30; Sat–Sun 09:30–12:30, 14:00–18:30; €5, guided visit €8 — check before you go.

name: Il Giogo Pass and Monte Altuzzo
text: Here US II Corps broke the Gothic Line in the central Apennines in September 1944, after six days of fighting up Monte Altuzzo and Monticelli against German paratroopers. The breakthrough outflanked the stronger Futa Pass. A 5.2 km waymarked Gothic Line ring trail from the pass leads to trenches and positions on Monte Altuzzo.
look: Stand at the pass and trace the skyline positions; with 2.5 hours to spare, walk the ring trail Passo del Giogo – Monte Altuzzo – Fonte Fredda.
plan: Parking at the pass on the SP503 between Scarperia and Firenzuola; trail moderate, 213 m of climb; wear boots.

name: German War Cemetery, Futa Pass
text: Italy's largest German war cemetery holds more than 30,600 dead, gathered from across the region, in terraces spiralling up a hilltop on the old Gothic Line. Designed by Dieter Oesterlen and dedicated in 1969, its 2 km stone wall climbs to a sharp prow-like summit. The graves are of the defenders of the Line, and of men from every Italian front after Rome.
look: Follow the spiral wall to the top for the view over the Futa and Giogo passes; note how young most of the men were.
plan: Via San Jacopo a Castro, Traversa (Firenzuola), on the SS65 at the Futa Pass. Open daily, free; hours vary by season — check before you go.

name: Monte Sole Historical Park — Casaglia
text: The heart of the Marzabotto massacre of 29 September to 5 October 1944. The Monte Sole Historical Park, created in 1989, preserves the ruins of hamlets, churches and farms where about 770 civilians were killed. At the church of Santa Maria Assunta in Casaglia, villagers who had taken refuge with their priest, Don Ubaldo Marchioni, were led into the cemetery and shot.
look: Walk the short way from the road to the Casaglia church ruins and cemetery; longer marked paths link San Martino, Caprara and Cerpiano.
plan: Park roads are narrow; allow time. The Il Poggiolo visitor centre and the Scuola di Pace Monte Sole offer guided visits — book ahead.

name: Sacrario dei Caduti, Marzabotto
text: Inaugurated in the early 1960s in the crypt of the parish church of Saints Joseph and Charles, the shrine holds the remains of hundreds of victims of the Monte Sole massacre and of partisans killed in the area. Plaques honour those decorated for their sacrifice, among them the priest Don Giovanni Fornasini and the Stella Rossa commander Mario 'Lupo' Musolesi.
look: Read the names on the tombs of the crypt; the paintings and bronzes by Stella Angelini depict the war, the massacre and the Resistance.
plan: Via Aldo Moro, Marzabotto town centre. Daily about 09:00–12:00 and 15:00–17:00 — check before you go.

name: Sacrario dei Partigiani, Piazza del Nettuno, Bologna
text: On 21 April 1945, the day Bologna was liberated, families began pinning photographs of their dead to the wall of Palazzo d'Accursio, where many partisans had been executed. The permanent memorial by Giuseppe Vaccaro, opened on 25 April 1955, holds more than 2,000 ceramic tiles with names and faces of partisans who died between 1943 and 1945.
look: Look for the photographs among the tiles, then walk into Piazza Maggiore, where Allied tanks and partisans were cheered on liberation day.
plan: City centre, always visible; Bologna has a limited-traffic zone, so leave the car at your campsite or a car park.

name: Polish War Cemetery, Bologna (San Lazzaro)
text: Here lie 1,432 soldiers of General Anders' Polish II Corps who died in 1944–45, many in the last offensive and the drive on Bologna, which Polish troops entered on 21 April 1945. The inscription reads that they fell on Italian soil fighting for a free Poland, a cause that, for most of them, the peace did not deliver.
look: Note the different headstone shapes for the soldiers' different faiths, and the ages: many were deportees released from the Soviet Union in 1942.
plan: Via Giuseppe Dozza, on the eastern edge of Bologna near the A14 San Lazzaro exit; free. The Museo Memoriale della Libertà (Via Dozza 24) nearby opens by appointment — check before you go.

name: Gradara War Cemetery
text: The cemetery holds 1,191 Commonwealth burials (and one Belgian) from the advance from Ancona to Rimini, which broke the Gothic Line, and from the heavy fighting around Rimini until its capture on 21 September 1944. Canadian, British and other Commonwealth soldiers who fought through this coastal sector lie side by side.
look: Walk the terraces, then look up at the medieval castle of Gradara on its hill above the coast road.
plan: On the SS16 between Cattolica and Pesaro (A14 exit Cattolica, follow Gradara then SS16 towards Pesaro); free, open access.

name: Montegridolfo and the Museo della Linea dei Goti
text: The walled hilltop village taken on 31 August 1944, where Lieutenant Gerard Norton won the Victoria Cross. A small local museum 300 metres from the centre gathers newspapers, photographs, weapons and everyday objects from 1943–44, many donated by villagers, telling the story of the Gothic Line from both sides and from the civilians caught between them.
look: Walk the walls for the view over the Foglia valley, then visit the museum on Via Borgo.
plan: Museo della Linea dei Goti, Via Borgo; admission by donation; opening days are limited — phone +39 0541 1613093 before you go.

name: Gemmano — "the Cassino of the Adriatic"
text: Between 4 and 15 September 1944 this hilltop village and the heights around it were attacked again and again by British 46th and 56th Divisions before the 4th Indian Division took the last positions on 15 September. The German mountain troops holding it suffered heavily, and more than 100 villagers were killed, many by naval shelling.
look: From the village look out over Zollara and the surrounding knolls and spurs, which changed hands repeatedly.
plan: Small village on narrow roads west of Morciano di Romagna; park in the centre and walk.

name: Coriano Ridge War Cemetery
text: The largest Commonwealth cemetery of the Adriatic Gothic Line: 1,939 burials, among them 1,413 British, 427 Canadian, 52 New Zealand and 28 South African. It lies on the slopes of the ridge fought over from 4 to 13 September 1944; in the week after its capture Eighth Army was losing some 150 killed a day. The cemetery was begun in April 1945.
look: Read the Canadian headstones from the 5th Armoured Division's assault, then look up the slope towards Coriano village on the crest.
plan: Via Piane, Coriano, 3.5 km west of Riccione, reached by turning west off the Rimini–Riccione road; free, open access.

name: Rimini Gurkha War Cemetery, Cerasolo
text: A quiet cemetery of 618 soldiers of the Indian Army, many of them Gurkhas, who died in the autumn 1944 fighting around Rimini and San Marino. It also holds the Rimini Cremation Memorial, one of three in Italy, naming 172 soldiers of the Indian Army whose bodies were cremated in accordance with their faith.
look: Look for the cremation memorial and the Nepali names on the Gurkha headstones; San Marino rises to the south-west.
plan: Via Consolare Rimini–San Marino, Cerasolo (Coriano); free, open access.

name: Rimini — the liberated city
text: Rimini was bombed from November 1943 onwards and about 82 per cent of its buildings were destroyed, the highest share among Italy's larger cities. On the morning of 21 September 1944 the 3rd Greek Mountain Brigade, fighting with I Canadian Corps, entered the abandoned city; the brigade was afterwards known as the Rimini Brigade.
look: Cross the Roman Tiberius bridge, which survived the war, and walk the old centre looking for the many plain post-war buildings between the monuments.
plan: Historic centre is a limited-traffic zone; park outside it. Good evening stop before the campsite.

name: Museo della Battaglia del Senio, Alfonsine
text: For the winter of 1944–45 the front lay along the high embankments of the Senio, with Germans and Allies sometimes on opposite sides of the same levee. Alfonsine was liberated on 10 April 1945, the day after the final offensive began. The museum, founded in 1981, covers the Allied operations, the Romagna partisans and civilian life under occupation.
look: Study the maps of the Senio front and the photographs of Kangaroo and Fantail vehicles used in the flooded plain.
plan: Piazza della Resistenza 2, Alfonsine. Mon–Fri 08:30–13:00, Wed also 14:00–17:00, Sat 09:00–12:00, Sun on request, closed in August; free — check before you go.

name: Lake Comacchio — the commandos' battlefield
text: In early April 1945 British commandos and the Special Boat Service opened the offensive on the spit and lagoons of Lake Comacchio. Corporal Tom Hunter of 43 Commando and Major Anders Lassen, a Dane serving with the SBS, won posthumous Victoria Crosses here; both are buried at Argenta. The lagoon's eastern side became the right flank of the drive on Argenta.
look: From Comacchio, drive the lagoon roads and imagine assault boats stuck in the shallows by night, as they were during the raid.
plan: Comacchio town is a good base for walking the lagoon edges; the lagoons are protected wetland, so stay on roads and paths.

name: Argenta Gap War Cemetery
text: The cemetery of the last hard battle in Italy holds 625 Commonwealth burials, most of them men killed in the Argenta Gap and around Lake Comacchio in April 1945. Among them are Anders Lassen VC, Tom Hunter VC and the George Cross holder Arthur Banks, an RAF pilot who fought alongside Italian partisans.
look: Find the Victoria Cross headstones of Lassen and Hunter, then look east across the flat fields that the 78th and 56th Divisions crossed.
plan: Strada di Sant'Antonio, about 2 km north of Argenta: from the SS16 pass the town centre and follow signs to Bando; the entrance is about 800 m from the road across private land, and the barrier is usually open 08:00–19:30; free — check before you go.

name: Argenta — the Gap
text: Argenta sits on the narrow strip of dry ground between the Reno and the flooded Valli di Comacchio. Once British V Corps took the town on 18 April 1945, armour could pour through the Gap towards Ferrara and the Po, turning the whole German defence line along the rivers. The town was heavily damaged in the fighting.
look: From the Reno embankment at the edge of town, see how thin the corridor of dry land really is.
plan: Park in the centre; the river embankments can be walked on the service tracks.

name: The Po at Pontelagoscuro, Ferrara
text: By 23–24 April 1945 the German armies were pinned against the Po with every bridge down. Eighth Army's 8th Indian, 56th and 2nd New Zealand Divisions crossed from 24 April with little opposition, while upstream the 6th South African Armoured Division crossed with the US Fifth Army; the banks were littered with abandoned guns and vehicles. The Adige followed on 27 April.
look: Walk up the embankment and look across the river: several hundred metres of fast water that thousands of Germans tried to swim.
plan: Pontelagoscuro is on the SS16 just north of Ferrara; park near the embankment and use the cycle path.

name: San Benedetto Po — the 10th Mountain crossing
text: The first Allied crossing of the Po was made here by the US 10th Mountain Division on 23 April 1945, in assault boats, the day after reaching the river. Within days the division was pushing up Lake Garda towards the Alps. The town itself grew round the great Benedictine abbey of Polirone.
look: Stand on the embankment and picture boats pushing off under sporadic fire; then visit the abbey square.
plan: About 1 hr 15 min west of Ferrara; worth it only on a long trip or if continuing towards Mantua and Verona.

name: Brazilian Votive Monument, Pistoia
text: The Brazilian Expeditionary Force buried its dead here, 463 men, until they were repatriated to Rio de Janeiro in 1960. A modernist votive monument by Olavo Redig de Campos, opened in 1967, now marks the site, with the tomb of an unknown Brazilian soldier.
look: The open pavilion, the stone terraces of the former cemetery and the tomb of the unknown soldier.

name: Sant'Anna di Stazzema National Park of Peace
text: The mountain village where about 560 civilians, most of them women, children and elderly, were killed by SS troops in a single morning. The whole village is now a memorial, with a museum, the church square and an ossuary monument above the coast.
look: The church square where many were killed, the Via Crucis path and the ossuary monument overlooking the Versilia coast.

name: Sommocolonia — Lieutenant Fox memorial
text: In this Garfagnana hill village about 70 soldiers of the African-American 92nd 'Buffalo' Division and 25 Italian partisans were overrun on 26 December 1944. Lieutenant John Fox called artillery fire onto his own position to cover the withdrawal and was killed; his Medal of Honor came only in 1997.
look: The Memory Park at the ruined tower opposite the parish church, a 10-minute walk from the lower car park.

name: Museo Storico dello Sbarco in Sicilia 1943
text: The island's main museum of the 1943 campaign, opened in December 2002 in the Le Ciminiere cultural centre. Photographs, documents, uniforms and weapons from all sides are combined with walk-through reconstructions of wartime Sicilian life and a large exhibition of photographs by the American war photographer Phil Stern. A good overview before or after visiting the battlefields.

name: Museo della Fotografia Robert Capa
text: Opened on 1 October 2021 in the Palazzo Pretura, this small museum displays 62 prints, many little known, from Robert Capa's negatives of the Sicily campaign. His pictures of Troina's shattered streets and its civilians remain some of the most powerful images of the war in Italy. Combine it with a walk to the upper town.

name: Museo dello Sbarco e Salerno Capitale
text: Opened in September 2012 for the 69th anniversary of the landings, this museum displays about 200 items on Operation Avalanche and on Salerno as seat of the Badoglio and Bonomi governments in 1944. Uniforms and weapons of all three armies, a Sherman tank, a jeep and a deportation wagon. Visits by reservation only.

name: Archaeological Park and Museum of Paestum
text: Not a war museum, but the temples stood in the middle of the American beachhead in September 1943 and both sides spared them. The museum's painted Tomb of the Diver is world famous. Combine with the 36th Division memorial on the beach, 1 km away. Open daily.

name: Galleria Borbonica
text: A tunnel dug for King Ferdinand II in the 1850s and old aqueduct cisterns, used as an air-raid shelter by thousands of Neapolitans during the Allied bombing of 1940–1943. Beds, graffiti and household objects survive, along with cars and motorbikes dumped here after the war. Guided tours only, Friday to Sunday.

name: Royal Palace of Caserta
text: The Bourbon royal palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, housed Fifth Army and then Allied Force Headquarters. The surrender of the German and Italian Fascist forces in Italy was signed here on 29 April 1945. The visit is mainly the royal apartments and park, with little on the war, so read up before you go.

name: Monte Lungo war museum
text: A small museum beside the Italian military shrine, with documents, photographs, weapons, and Italian and Allied vehicles and guns from the battles of December 1943. It tells the story of the Italian 1st Motorised Group, the first unit of the new Italian army to fight alongside the Allies. Free entry; hours vary.

name: Museo Parco della Memoria Storica
text: Opened in December 2008 in a restored olive-oil mill, this immersive museum uses darkness, sound and seven staged scenes, including John Huston's 1943–44 film footage, to recount the battle and the destruction of the village. Weekend opening; weekdays by booking. Pair it with a walk through the ruins.

name: MUBA — Museo della Battaglia di Ortona
text: Founded in 2002, the museum has halls on the civilians, with photographs and a model of the destroyed centre, on the combatants, with objects donated by veterans, and on wartime propaganda. It remembers the 1,314 civilian dead as well as Canadian and German soldiers. Temporarily closed for renovation at last check.

name: Museo Linea Gustav
text: A local museum created by the Associazione Linea Gustav Fronte Garigliano and opened in recent years in the old centre. It gathers weapons, equipment, documents and photographs from the Garigliano front and gives particular weight to the civilians of Castelforte and neighbouring villages, whose homes were almost completely destroyed in 1944. Visits must be arranged in advance by phone or email.

name: Historiale di Cassino
text: Cassino's multimedia museum, opened in 2004 for the 60th anniversary of the battle and dedicated to the fallen of all nations. Rooms designed by Carlo Rambaldi take visitors through the Gustav Line, the bombing of the abbey, military strategy, civilian life and the rebuilding of the town. Guided visits run at set times on weekdays; check current hours before going.

name: Memorial Museum of the 2nd Polish Corps
text: Opened on 17 May 2014 for the battle's 70th anniversary, at the entrance to the Polish cemetery. Large photographic displays in Italian, Polish and English, films and battlefield relics follow General Anders' soldiers from Soviet captivity through Cassino to the liberation of Bologna in April 1945. It was funded by donors in the countries where many veterans settled after the war.

name: Museo dello Sbarco di Anzio
text: The Anzio landing museum in the 17th-century Villa Adele, opened for the 50th anniversary in 1994. Four sections (American, British, German and Italian) display uniforms, weapons, medals, documents, plans and photographs, plus finds recovered from the seabed, including from HMS Spartan and HMS Janus. Entry is free; opening days and afternoon hours vary, so check first.

name: Museo dello Sbarco Alleato
text: Nettuno's museum of Operation Shingle, housed in the Forte Sangallo, a seafront fortress of 1501. The collection covers the landing of 22 January 1944 and the beachhead battle with documents, furnishings, uniforms, helmets, period photographs, maps, war correspondents' reports, newspapers and objects found in the Anzio–Nettuno area. Free entry during opening hours.

name: Museo Piana delle Orme
text: A large private museum founded in 1997 by Mariano De Pasquale, with about 50,000 objects in many pavilions. Besides farming, toys and the draining of the Pontine marshes, it has major Second World War halls: dioramas of the Anzio landing (including the Rangers' battle at Cisterna) and Cassino, and a large collection of military vehicles. Adult ticket €13 in 2026.

name: Mausoleo delle Fosse Ardeatine and museum
text: The national memorial to the 335 victims of the massacre of 24 March 1944, inaugurated on 24 March 1949. Visitors enter by Mirko Basaldella's bronze gates, pass Francesco Coccia's sculpture of three bound men, walk through the quarry tunnels and reach the shrine of 335 granite tombs. A small museum explains the occupation, Via Rasella and the trials. Free.

name: Museo storico della Liberazione
text: Housed in the apartments at Via Tasso 145 that the German security police under Herbert Kappler used as a prison from 1943 to June 1944. Preserved cells with prisoners' graffiti, arrest files, photographs and documents tell the story of the occupation, the Resistance and the persecution of Rome's Jews. Donated to the state in 1950, it opened fully in 1957. Free.

name: Museo Storico della Resistenza, Sant'Anna di Stazzema
text: Opened in 1982 by President Sandro Pertini in the old village school, the museum tells the story of the war, the Resistance and the massacre of 12 August 1944 through photographs, testimonies and objects. It is part of the National Park of Peace, which includes the church square, the Via Crucis and the ossuary monument. Entry is free; check days before you go.

name: MuGot — Museo Gotica Toscana
text: Founded in 2019 between the Futa and Giogo passes, this volunteer museum collects documents, filmed testimonies, uniforms and equipment from the 1944 battles in the Mugello. Its guides run battlefield visits to the bunkers and trenches of the Gothic Line. Open Wednesday and Friday mornings and weekends; €5, guided tours extra.

name: Monte Sole Historical Park
text: A regional park created in 1989 on the massif where about 770 civilians were killed between 29 September and 5 October 1944. Marked paths link the ruined churches, hamlets and cemeteries of Casaglia, San Martino, Caprara and Cerpiano. The Scuola di Pace Monte Sole and the Il Poggiolo visitor centre run guided visits and education programmes.

name: Museo della Linea dei Goti
text: A small, heartfelt village museum on Via Borgo, built largely from objects donated by local families: newspapers, postcards, photographs, weapons, grenades and gas masks from 1943–44, plus period films. It explains the Gothic Line from the viewpoint of the valley that saw it broken. Admission by donation; opening days are limited, so phone ahead.

name: Museo della Battaglia del Senio
text: Founded in 1981 in the town liberated on 10 April 1945, the museum covers the winter front on the Senio embankments and the spring offensive, with weapons, uniforms, flags and photographs arranged along three paths: Allied operations, the partisans and civilian life. Free entry; weekday mornings, Wednesday afternoons, closed in August.

name: Syracuse War Cemetery
text: About 1,060 Commonwealth burials, mostly from the landings between Pachino and Syracuse and from the glider operation that ended in the sea. British, Indian, South African, Canadian and Australian graves lie side by side.
look: Glider Pilot Regiment and airlanding brigade headstones, the rows of Indian graves, and the Cross of Sacrifice near the entrance.

name: Catania War Cemetery
text: About 2,135 Commonwealth soldiers killed in the battles for the Simeto bridgehead and the Catania plain, including most of the 1st Parachute Brigade dead from Primosole and many men of the 50th and 51st Divisions.
look: The paratroopers' graves, the Durham Light Infantry headstones and the view of Etna over the plain.

name: Agira Canadian War Cemetery
text: The resting place of 490 Canadians who died in Sicily, gathered into a single cemetery after the campaign. It stands on a hill east of Agira, where the 1st Canadian Division fought its costliest battle of the campaign.
look: Terraced rows on the hilltop looking across Lake Pozzillo to Agira and Etna; the visitors' book.

name: German War Cemetery Motta Sant'Anastasia
text: 4,561 German soldiers killed in Sicily, 451 unknown, gathered into a walled building of five courtyards at the foot of Etna. It is maintained by the German war graves commission, the Volksbund.
look: Five raised courtyards, four named after Sicilian provinces,, the bronze memorial sculpture and the grave of Olympian Luz Long.

name: Sacrario di Cristo Re, Messina
text: Italy's military shrine in Messina holds 1,288 Italian dead of the Second World War and 110 of the First. Most of the Italian soldiers killed in Sicily lie in communal cemeteries or shrines elsewhere; this is the main one on the tour.
look: The crypt with its wall niches, the huge bell that rings at sunset and the view over the Strait.

name: 82nd Airborne memorial, Ponte Dirillo
text: The main US memorial to the campaign in Sicily, near Biazza Ridge; it names some 39 paratroopers. American dead from Sicily were moved to the Sicily-Rome American Cemetery at Nettuno, near Anzio, so there is no US war cemetery on the island.
look: The names tablet, the restored Italian bunkers of the Ponte Dirillo strongpoint and the view east to Biazza Ridge.

name: Primosole Bridge
text: The bridge over the Simeto where British and German paratroopers fought each other for three days. Its capture opened the Catania plain, but the German line beyond it held until early August.
look: The bridge, the flat river banks where the paratroops fought, and the roadside memorials to the fallen of all nations.

name: Salerno War Cemetery
cat: Sep 1943 · Commonwealth graves of the Salerno landings
text: Burial ground of 1,851 Commonwealth servicemen, most of them killed in the Salerno beachhead between 9 and 18 September 1943. The site was chosen in November 1943; later burials came from a wide area of south-west Italy and from the nearby 59th General Hospital.
look: Row upon row of X Corps headstones in a calm Louis de Soissons design, a few minutes from the old airfield.

name: San Pietro Infine ruins
cat: 8–17 Dec 1943 · village destroyed in the Winter Line
text: The abandoned ruins of a village fought over by the US 36th Division and the German 29th Panzergrenadier Division. Left as a memorial, it is one of the few places in Italy where the destruction of 1943 can still be seen as it was.
look: Roofless streets, the shattered church, and the caves where villagers sheltered through weeks of shelling in December 1943.

name: Italian military shrine of Monte Lungo
cat: 8 & 16 Dec 1943 · the new Italian army’s first battle
text: The shrine holds 974 Italian dead, 784 of them from the battles of Monte Lungo and Cassino. It marks the moment Italian troops returned to battle on the Allied side, at a heavy cost, three months after the armistice.
look: Terraced graves facing the bare ridge of Monte Lungo, with the museum and its vehicles across the Via Casilina.

name: Royal Palace of Caserta
cat: Oct 1943 – May 1945 · Allied HQ; surrender signed 29 Apr 1945
text: From the autumn of 1943 the palace housed the US Fifth Army's headquarters, and later Allied Force Headquarters. On 29 April 1945 German envoys signed the surrender of German and Italian Fascist forces in Italy here, effective on 2 May, a week before the general German surrender.
look: The royal apartments, the grand staircase and the long park where Allied soldiers once camped and rested.

name: Sangro River War Cemetery
cat: Nov 1943 – 1944 · British, New Zealand and Indian graves
text: With 2,617 burials, the Commonwealth's main cemetery for the Adriatic winter of 1943–44. It includes the Sangro River Cremation Memorial to more than 500 Indian soldiers, and graves of escaped prisoners of war killed trying to reach Allied lines.
look: The cremation memorial, the New Zealand silver fern on headstones, and the German-held ridge across the river.

name: Moro River Canadian War Cemetery
text: Canada's largest war cemetery in Italy: 1,615 graves, 1,375 of them Canadian, from the Moro, the Gully and Ortona. It was begun in January 1944, on high ground between the battlefield and the town the Canadians took.
look: Terraces of maple-leaf headstones, with the Moro valley below and the town of Ortona to the north.

name: Ortona
text: The Adriatic port where the 1st Canadian Division and the German 1st Parachute Division fought an eight-day street battle. About 80 per cent of the town was destroyed and 1,314 civilians died; the town received the Gold Medal for Civil Valour.
look: The Corso, the rebuilt cathedral of San Tommaso and the castle over the harbour, all reconstructed after 1943.

name: Abbey of Monte Cassino
text: The Benedictine mother house founded around 529 sat on the height that dominated the road to Rome. Its destruction by 229 Allied bombers on 15 February 1944 killed civilians sheltering inside, handed the Germans a ready-made fortress and remains the campaign's most debated decision. Rebuilt, it was reconsecrated in 1964.
look: Photographs of the ruins, the rebuilt basilica and the terrace view over the Liri valley and the town.

name: Polish War Cemetery, Monte Cassino
text: Built by the Polish II Corps between 1944 and 1946 on the slope between Point 593 and the abbey, it holds just over 1,000 soldiers (sources give 1,051 to 1,072). General Anders was buried here beside his men in 1970. For Poles it is one of the most important national shrines outside Poland.
look: The terraces, the tall cross with the Polish eagle, Anders' grave and the memorial museum at the entrance.

name: Cassino War Cemetery and Memorial
text: The largest Commonwealth war cemetery in Italy, designed by Louis de Soissons, with 4,271 burials (289 unidentified). The Cassino Memorial within it names more than 4,000 Commonwealth soldiers of the whole Italian campaign who have no known grave, including 194 Canadians.
look: The green memorial panels, the Indian and Gurkha graves, and the view of the abbey above.

name: German War Cemetery, Caira
text: Laid out by the Volksbund on Colle Marino north of Cassino and inaugurated on 4 May 1965, it holds about 20,000 German dead of the southern Italian campaign, 3,100 of them unidentified, reburied here from field graves in 1959–60.
look: Terraces of stone crosses rising to a bronze cross, with a wide view of the Rapido valley.

name: French Military Cemetery, Venafro
text: The largest French war cemetery in Italy, for soldiers of General Juin's French Expeditionary Corps, most of them North African. Published figures differ: 3,414 graves in several heritage listings, about 5,200 in French sources since graves from the Miano cemetery in Naples were moved here in 1990–91. Their breakthrough in the Aurunci in May 1944 decided the battle for the Gustav Line.
look: Rows of crosses and Muslim headstones, and the names of the Moroccan, Algerian and Tunisian regiments.

name: Beach Head War Cemetery, Anzio
text: The main Commonwealth cemetery of the Anzio beachhead, with 2,316 burials, 2,025 of them identified, mostly British soldiers killed in the February and March battles along the Via Anziate, with Canadians, South Africans and others among them. It stands on the road the German offensive was trying to reach.
look: The Guards and London regiment graves, the personal inscriptions, and the view inland towards Aprilia.

name: Sicily–Rome American Cemetery, Nettuno
text: Dedicated in 1956 on 77 acres at Nettuno, it holds 7,858 American war dead from Sicily to just north of Rome, with the names of 3,095 missing on the chapel walls. A visitor centre opened in 2014 explains the campaign.
look: The curving rows under Roman pines, the chapel, the map room and the visitor centre.

name: Mausoleo delle Fosse Ardeatine, Rome
text: The site of the worst German massacre in occupied Rome, carried out in reprisal for the Via Rasella attack. The memorial of 1949 is a landmark of Italian postwar architecture and the focus of national remembrance every 24 March.
look: The quarry tunnels, the bronze gates, the sculpture of three men and the shrine of 335 tombs.

name: Florence American Cemetery and Memorial
text: The American Battle Monuments Commission cemetery for the campaign north of Rome: 4,402 graves on curved terraces in the Greve valley and 1,409 names on the Tablets of the Missing. The memorial chapel and map room tell the story of Fifth Army from Rome to the Alps.
look: Operations maps in the memorial, the Tablets of the Missing with rosettes for men later found, and the terraces seen from the top.

name: Coriano Ridge War Cemetery
text: The main Commonwealth cemetery of Operation Olive, with 1,939 burials: British, 427 Canadians, New Zealanders, South Africans and Indians. It lies on the ridge that blocked Eighth Army's road to Rimini for nine days in September 1944.
look: The Canadian plots, and the view up the slope to Coriano village on the crest.

name: German War Cemetery, Futa Pass
text: Italy's largest German war cemetery, built on the Gothic Line at the Futa Pass and dedicated in 1969. Its spiralling stone wall and hilltop crypt make it one of the most striking war cemeteries in Europe.
look: The 2 km spiral wall, the crypt at the summit and the view over both Apennine passes.

name: Polish War Cemetery, Bologna
text: The resting place of 1,432 men of the Polish II Corps killed in 1944–45, including the last battles for Bologna, which Polish troops were among the first to enter on 21 April 1945.
look: The entrance inscription to the soldiers of II Corps who fell on Italian soil fighting for a free Poland.

name: Brazilian Votive Monument, Pistoia
text: The Brazilian Expeditionary Force buried its dead here, 463 men, until they were repatriated to Rio de Janeiro in 1960. A modernist votive monument by Olavo Redig de Campos, opened in 1967, now marks the site, with the tomb of an unknown Brazilian soldier.
look: The open pavilion, the stone terraces of the former cemetery and the tomb of the unknown soldier.

name: Sant'Anna di Stazzema National Park of Peace
text: The mountain village where about 560 civilians, most of them women, children and elderly, were killed by SS troops in a single morning. The whole village is now a memorial, with a museum, the church square and an ossuary monument above the coast.
look: The church square where many were killed, the Via Crucis path and the ossuary monument overlooking the Versilia coast.

name: Sommocolonia — Lieutenant Fox memorial
text: In this Garfagnana hill village about 70 soldiers of the African-American 92nd 'Buffalo' Division and 25 Italian partisans were overrun on 26 December 1944. Lieutenant John Fox called artillery fire onto his own position to cover the withdrawal and was killed; his Medal of Honor came only in 1997.
look: The Memory Park at the ruined tower opposite the parish church, a 10-minute walk from the lower car park.

name: Ponte Grande — gliders seize the bridge
text: Operation Ladbroke sent 144 gliders of the British 1st Airlanding Brigade to seize this bridge over the Anapo south of Syracuse. In a gale, 65 came down in the sea and some 252 men drowned; only a handful landed near the target. A single platoon of the South Staffords took the bridge and, reinforced to about 87 men, held it until mid-afternoon. The Royal Scots Fusiliers of 5th Division retook it intact at 16:15.
look: The road bridge over the Anapo and the flat, canal-cut ground around it. Imagine the few glider men firing from the ditches, with Syracuse harbour behind you.

name: Gela — Rangers and 1st Division storm ashore
text: At 02:45 the US 1st Infantry Division landed on the beaches east of Gela while Darby's 1st and 4th Ranger Battalions went straight at the town, whose pier the Italians blew up. The destroyer USS Maddox was sunk offshore by an air attack just before 05:00. That morning nine or ten Italian tanks of Mobile Group E dashed into Gela's streets before Rangers and engineers drove them out with bazookas and grenades.
look: Stand on the seafront by the pier and look along the flat beaches to the east, where the landing craft grounded, then up at the old town on its low ridge.

name: Bark West — the Canadians land near Pachino
text: The 1st Canadian Infantry Division (Major-General Guy Simonds) and the 1st Canadian Army Tank Brigade came ashore on 'Bark West' beach near Maucini, with Royal Marine Nos. 40 and 41 Commandos landing alongside. Opposition from the Italian coastal troops was light and Pachino was reached the same day. It was the start of a month-long campaign that cost Canada some 562 dead.
look: A low, sandy beach at the south-eastern tip of Sicily, today marked only by a Canadian flag. Look west along the Roger and Sugar sectors.

name: Piano Lupo — the Gela counterattack
text: At 06:15 the Hermann Göring Panzer Division and the Italian Livorno Division struck at the Gela beachhead. German tanks rolled down the Niscemi road past Piano Lupo, held by the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the 16th Infantry with scattered paratroopers of the 505th, and across the Gela plain to within about 2,000 yards of the water. Artillery landed by DUKW, anti-tank guns and naval gunfire stopped them; sixteen German tanks were left burning and the attack was called off after 14:00.
look: The junction where the Niscemi road meets the SS115. Some Italian concrete pillboxes survive on the slope among greenhouses; look south across the plain to the sea.

name: Biazza Ridge — Gavin stops the Tigers
text: Colonel James Gavin, commander of the 505th Parachute Infantry, gathered paratroopers, engineers, cooks and clerks on this low ridge east of the Acate river and met a German battle group with Tiger tanks. Pack howitzers fired over open sights; in the evening, reinforced by Sherman tanks, Gavin counterattacked and the Germans fell back. The stand stopped the eastern arm of the counterattack and won Gavin the Distinguished Service Cross.
look: Look east from the Ponte Dirillo memorial along the SS115 to the low ridge line among vineyards and greenhouses, about three kilometres away.

name: Primosole Bridge — paratroops against paratroops
