text: Operation Fustian dropped the British 1st Parachute Brigade to seize this bridge over the Simeto, the gateway to the Catania plain. Scattered by flak, including Allied naval fire, only about 295 of 1,856 men reached the objective. They took the bridge but were driven off on 14 July by German paratroopers. The Durham Light Infantry of 50th Division needed until 16 July to secure it; the plain beyond held Eighth Army for three weeks.
look: The SS114 still crosses the Simeto here. Look at the flat riverbanks and the roadside memorial to the fallen of all nations; Etna rises to the north.

name: Palermo falls; three days later Mussolini is deposed
text: Patton's Provisional Corps swept across western Sicily and at 19:00 on 22 July accepted Palermo's surrender at the royal palace; Patton arrived that night. The drive took some 53,000 prisoners, mostly Italian. In Rome the Fascist Grand Council voted 19 to 8 against Mussolini in the early hours of 25 July, and that afternoon the King dismissed and arrested him. Marshal Badoglio's new government announced that the war would go on.
look: The Norman royal palace, today Sicily's regional parliament. Palermo is off the three-day route; a separate city visit shows the palace, the port and the bomb-scarred old quarters.

name: Agira — the Canadians' hardest fight
text: Advancing east from Leonforte, the 1st Canadian Division attacked Agira, a hill town held by German Panzergrenadiers. Five days of fighting through Nissoria and along the surrounding ridges, ending in house-to-house combat, cost the division about 438 casualties, its heaviest of the Sicilian campaign. The town fell on 28 July, opening the road east towards Regalbuto and Adrano and the western end of the German Etna line.
look: The steep hill town with its castle on top. From the Canadian War Cemetery east of the town, look back at the ridges the battalions climbed.

name: Troina — the battle of the Big Red One
text: At 1,100 metres, Troina anchored the western end of the German Etna line. The US 1st Infantry Division under Terry Allen, with the 39th Infantry and a Moroccan Tabor of Goums, attacked the German 15th Panzergrenadier Division and Italian troops of the Aosta Division. The defenders made about two dozen counterattacks; bombers and artillery wrecked the town. The Germans slipped away on the night of 5–6 August; Allen was relieved of command soon afterwards.
look: The ridge-top town with views over the hills the infantry crossed. Robert Capa's photographs of the ruined town and its civilians hang in the museum here.

name: Brolo — Patton's end run behind the lines
text: To outflank the German line on the Naso ridge, Patton put Lieutenant Colonel Lyle Bernard's 2nd Battalion, 30th Infantry, with tanks and two artillery batteries, ashore behind the enemy at Brolo. They seized Monte Cipolla above the coast road and, supported by the cruiser USS Philadelphia, held out all day against counterattacks by the 29th Panzergrenadier Division. Relieved at 07:30 on 12 August, the force had lost 177 men.
look: The steep hill between the Naso and Brolo rivers that overlooks the coast road and railway. Imagine the landing craft on the beach below.

name: The Strait — the Axis gets away
text: In Operation Lehrgang German ferries, landing craft and barges carried troops from the beaches north of Messina to Calabria night after night from 11 to 17 August, under an umbrella of some 500 anti-aircraft guns. The Allied air forces and navies failed to stop them. Estimates run from about 40,000 to 60,000 German troops, with some 10,000 vehicles, plus 62,000–75,000 Italians carried in their own operation. The same divisions would fight at Salerno.
look: At Torre Faro the Strait is only about three kilometres wide. Look across at the Calabrian shore at Villa San Giovanni and picture the nightly shuttle.

name: Messina — Patton wins the race
text: A patrol of the US 3rd Division's 7th Infantry entered the bomb-wrecked city on the evening of 16 August. At 10:00 next morning Patton drove down from the hills to accept its surrender, just ahead of British commandos arriving from the south. The last German boats had left hours earlier. The 38-day campaign was over; Allied troops crossed the Strait to Calabria on 3 September.
look: From the terrace of the Cristo Re shrine you see the harbour, the city rebuilt after the bombing, and the Calabrian coast across the Strait.

name: Reggio Calabria — Eighth Army crosses to the mainland
text: Before dawn on 3 September 1943, after a barrage from more than 600 guns firing across the Strait of Messina, British XIII Corps landed on the beaches north of Reggio in Operation Baytown: the 1st Canadian Division aimed for Reggio and its airfield, the British 5th Division for Villa San Giovanni. The Germans had already pulled back, and Italian coastal troops surrendered. Six days later the British 1st Airborne Division sailed into Taranto (Operation Slapstick).
look: Stand on the Gallico–Catona shore and look across the narrow strait to Sicily, where the guns were lined up. The ferry you arrived on crosses roughly the same water.

name: Paestum beaches — US 36th Division lands at Salerno
text: Hours after the Italian armistice was announced on the evening of 8 September, the US 36th Infantry Division, in battle for the first time, landed on four beaches (Red, Green, Yellow, Blue) below the Greek temples of Paestum at 03:30. There was no preliminary bombardment, and the 16th Panzer Division was waiting. By nightfall the Texans held Capaccio and the slopes of Monte Soprano, at a cost of about 500 casualties.
look: The flat beach, the pine belt behind it and the medieval Torre di Paestum are much as the assault waves saw them. Look inland to the temples and the grey ridge of Monte Soprano.

name: Battipaglia — British X Corps fights for the northern plain
text: North of the Sele, the British 46th and 56th Divisions of X Corps landed on 9 September while Commandos seized Vietri and US Rangers the passes above Maiori. The 56th took Montecorvino airfield and on 10 September pushed into Battipaglia, a vital road junction, but was thrown out that evening; after two more days of fighting, German counter-attacks drove the division off the edge of the town on 12 September. The British held on just south of the town; Battipaglia, largely destroyed, was finally entered on 18 September.
look: Modern Battipaglia was rebuilt almost from scratch. From the SS18 look north to the airport (the old Montecorvino airfield) and east to the hills that gave German observers their view.

name: Altavilla and Hill 424 — the heights above the beachhead
text: The hill village of Altavilla and Hill 424 behind it overlook the whole Sele plain. Men of the 36th Division occupied the village by 11 September, lost it to German counter-attacks on 12 September, and failed to retake Hill 424 the next day; the 1st Battalion, 142nd Infantry was almost destroyed. Naval gunfire and bombing wrecked the village, and 85 civilians died on its territory. The Americans only reoccupied it on 18–19 September.
look: From the upper village look west over the plain to the sea: this is the view that let German gunners direct fire onto every beach and road. Hill 424 rises just behind the houses.

name: Sele–Calore corridor — the German counter-attack is stopped
text: At 15:30 on 13 September German tanks and infantry drove down the corridor between the Sele and Calore rivers, into a gap between the US and British corps. The 2nd Battalion, 143rd Infantry was overrun, and the attack headed for the beaches. Near a burned bridge over the Calore, the 158th and 189th Field Artillery Battalions fired about 3,650 rounds in four hours, their crews fighting as infantry. It was the crisis of the Salerno battle.
look: Flat farmland of buffalo-milk dairies and tomato fields between two tree-lined rivers: imagine it without cover, the guns firing over open sights from the low ground near La Cosa creek.

name: Naples — the Four Days and the arrival of the Allies
text: After the German commandant, Colonel Walter Schöll, declared a state of siege and ordered men aged 18–33 to report for labour, Neapolitans rose up on 27 September. For four days civilians, soldiers and teenagers fought German troops in the Vomero, Materdei, Capodimonte and elsewhere. Death tolls vary widely: from 155 to more than 600 Italians, and several dozen Germans. On 1 October British armoured cars of the King's Dragoon Guards entered a city with a wrecked port.
look: The stone panels of Marino Mazzacurati's monument (inaugurated 1969) show fighters of every age. It is popularly, if loosely, called the monument to the scugnizzo, the street boy, though it honours all who fought.

name: Volturno — Fifth Army crosses the river in flood
text: The Volturno, swollen by autumn rain, was the first German river line north of Naples. At 01:00 on 13 October Fifth Army's guns opened fire and six divisions, three American and three British, attacked. The US 3rd Division feinted at the Triflisco gap and crossed near Monte Caruso; the 34th took Caiazzo. The British 56th Division failed at Capua and later used an American bridge, while the 46th crossed near the sea. The Germans fell back to the Barbara Line.
look: Near Capua the river runs deep between high banks, 45–65 metres wide. Picture assault boats and rafts crossing in the dark under fire from the ridges to the north.

name: Sangro River — Eighth Army storms the Adriatic end of the Winter Line
text: On the Adriatic, Montgomery's Eighth Army reached the Sangro in November. Small bridgeheads had been won by 24 November and, after days of rain and flooding, the main attack by the British 78th Division, 8th Indian Division and 2nd New Zealand Division took the ridge beyond the river by nightfall on 30 November. The German 65th Infantry Division was badly mauled, but mud, rain and fresh German divisions slowed the advance towards the Moro and Ortona.
look: The war cemetery sits on the valley floor facing the ridge the Germans held. Look north-west up the Sangro to Mozzagrogna and Fossacesia on the heights above the river.

name: Monte la Difensa — the Special Service Force climbs the cliffs
text: Operation Raincoat opened Fifth Army's attack on the Winter Line at the Mignano gap. On the night of 2–3 December the US–Canadian 1st Special Service Force scaled the cliffs of Monte la Difensa (Hill 960) and took the summit at dawn, while the British 56th Division fought for Monte Camino (Hill 963), secured on 6 December. In six days of cold and rain the Force suffered 511 casualties, including 73 dead.
look: The summit, reached by a steep hike of several hours, carries memorials to the Force. From the valley, look at the rock faces the men climbed with ropes at night.

name: Moro River and Casa Berardi — Canada’s December battle
text: The 1st Canadian Division crossed the Moro on 6–9 December at Villa Rogatti, San Leonardo and near the coast, then ran into 'the Gully', a ravine about 60 metres deep held by German paratroopers and panzergrenadiers. On 14 December Captain Paul Triquet's company of the Royal 22e Régiment fought through to the farmhouse of Casa Berardi, reaching it with only 14 to 17 men fit to fight (sources differ). Triquet received the Victoria Cross. The Germans left the Gully on 20 December.
look: Casa Berardi is a private farmhouse with a memorial at the gate; view it from the road. The flat fields around it were the killing ground between the Gully and the crossroads.

name: San Pietro Infine — a village destroyed in the Winter Line
text: San Pietro sat on the slopes of Monte Sammucro, covering the road through the Mignano gap. From 8 December the US 36th Division attacked across terraced olive groves; on the same day the Italian 1st Motorised Group made its first attack for the Allies, on nearby Monte Lungo, and failed. A tank attack on 15 December lost 12 of 16 Shermans. The Germans withdrew on the night of 16–17 December, leaving the village in ruins.
look: The old village was never rebuilt: walk its roofless streets, church and cave shelters. John Huston filmed the battle here, and the museum screens his footage.

name: Ortona — street fighting in “Little Stalingrad”
text: From 20 December the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada, with Three Rivers tanks, fought house by house against the German 1st Parachute Division. Streets were rubble-blocked and mined, so the Canadians 'mouse-holed', blasting through walls from house to house. On Christmas Day companies rotated through a dinner in the church of Santa Maria di Costantinopoli. The paratroopers withdrew on the night of 27–28 December. 1,314 of Ortona's people died in the battle and the bombardments.
look: Walk Corso Vittorio Emanuele, the Canadians' main axis, to the rebuilt cathedral of San Tommaso, which German engineers blew up on 21 December 1943, according to most accounts (some blame Allied shelling). Most of the old town was rebuilt after the war.

name: Garigliano, Minturno — British X Corps crosses the river
text: At 21:00 on 17 January 1944 British X Corps opened the first battle for the Gustav Line. The 5th and 56th (London) Infantry Divisions crossed the fast, flooded Garigliano near its mouth, in assault boats and DUKWs, and fought their way up to Minturno, Tufo and the slopes towards Castelforte. The bridgehead held, but cost about 4,000 casualties in the first weeks. Alarmed, Kesselring rushed two panzergrenadier divisions south from Rome, just before the Anzio landing.
look: Stand by the restored Real Ferdinando suspension bridge beside the Roman ruins of Minturnae. Look north to the hill town of Minturno: every ridge between the river and the town was fought over.

name: Sant'Angelo in Theodice — the US 36th Division fails at the Rapido
text: On the foggy night of 20 January the 141st and 143rd Infantry Regiments of the US 36th (Texas) Division tried to cross the Gari (Rapido) river on either side of Sant'Angelo in Theodice, under German guns on the far bank. Boats were holed, footbridges broke and minefields waited on both banks. After two nights the survivors were back where they started. Sources give between about 1,700 and 2,100 American casualties in 48 hours, against light German losses.
look: From the piazza memorials look down on the narrow, fast river and the flat meadows on the far side, with Monte Cassino filling the skyline to the north.

name: Anzio — Operation Shingle lands behind the Gustav Line
text: At 02:00 on 22 January 1944 US VI Corps under Major General John P. Lucas landed at Anzio and Nettuno, about 60 km south of Rome: the British 1st Infantry Division north of the town, US Rangers and paratroopers at the harbour, and the US 3rd Infantry Division to the east. Surprise was complete. By midnight some 36,000 men and 3,200 vehicles were ashore for 13 killed. Lucas dug in rather than dash inland, and the Germans reacted fast.
look: Walk the harbour front of Anzio, where the Rangers and the 509th Parachute Infantry Battalion came ashore, then imagine hundreds of ships lying off this flat coast.

name: Cisterna — two Ranger battalions destroyed
text: Before dawn on 30 January the 1st and 3rd Ranger Battalions crept along a drainage ditch towards Cisterna, leading a US 3rd Division attack. At first light they were caught in open fields near Isola Bella by German troops and tanks. Of 767 Rangers, only six got back to Allied lines; the rest were killed or captured. The same day the British 1st Division pushed towards Campoleone but ended in an exposed salient. The beachhead was now under siege.
look: At the roadside Rangers memorial near Isola Bella, look across the flat, open farmland of the reclaimed Pontine marshes: there was nowhere to hide once day broke.

name: Monte Cassino — the abbey is destroyed from the air
text: On the morning of 15 February 1944, at the request of the New Zealand Corps, 229 American bombers (142 B-17s, 47 B-25s and 40 B-26s) dropped about 1,150 tonnes of bombs on the 6th-century Benedictine abbey, and artillery joined in. Allied commanders believed German troops were using it. They were not: the abbey was sheltering civilians, of whom about 230 died by one widely cited count. German troops then moved into the ruins and made them a fortress.
look: From the rebuilt cloisters look down the 500 m drop to Cassino town and the Liri valley: you see exactly why both sides thought this height controlled the road to Rome.

name: Aprilia, 'the Factory' — the German counter-offensive
text: The brick-built new town of Aprilia, called 'the Factory' by Allied soldiers, and nearby Carroceto were lost by the British 1st Division on 9–10 February. On 16 February General von Mackensen's Fourteenth Army launched Operation Fischfang down the Via Anziate, the Albano–Anzio road, to split the beachhead. For four days British and American troops held on near the Flyover bridge, helped by massed artillery and bombers, and the attack was stopped only a few kilometres from the sea.
look: Stand on Aprilia's central square, rebuilt after the war, and look south along the straight Via Anziate towards Anzio: this was the axis of every German attack.

name: Cassino town and Castle Hill — the third battle
text: From 08:30 on 15 March 1944 Allied bombers dropped about 750 tonnes of bombs on Cassino town for three and a half hours, followed by a massive artillery barrage. The 2nd New Zealand Division attacked through the rubble and took Castle Hill (Rocca Janula); Gurkhas of the 4th Indian Division reached Hangman's Hill just below the abbey. But German paratroopers survived in cellars and ruins, rain flooded the craters and tanks could not pass. The battle was called off on 23 March.
look: From the walls of the Rocca Janula look up to the abbey and across the town below: the Continental Hotel, the railway station and Hangman's Hill are all in view.

name: Fosse Ardeatine, Rome — 335 men murdered in reprisal
text: On 23 March 1944 Roman partisans of the GAP exploded a bomb in Via Rasella, killing 33 men of the German police regiment 'Bozen'. Within 24 hours, on Hitler's order, passed down through Kesselring and General von Mackensen, SS officer Herbert Kappler had 335 men and boys taken to disused quarries on the Via Ardeatina and shot in the back of the head, five more than the ten-for-one ratio demanded. The victims included 75 Jews. The caves were then blown shut.
look: Walk through the tunnels where the shootings took place and into the low, dim shrine where the 335 lie in identical granite tombs under a single vast concrete slab.

name: Monte Maio — the French break through the Aurunci mountains
text: Operation Diadem opened at 23:00 on 11 May with more than 1,600 guns. While the British and Poles were held at Cassino, General Alphonse Juin's French Expeditionary Corps, mostly Moroccan and Algerian troops, stormed the Aurunci mountains. Monte Maio fell on 13 May and the Moroccan goumiers then crossed trackless heights behind the German line. This was the decisive breakthrough. In the villages beyond, such as Esperia, the following days also brought the Marocchinate: mass rapes and killings of Italian civilians by some of these troops.
look: Monte Maio (940 m) is the high summit north of Castelforte and Ausonia. From the Ausonia road, look at the steep, scrubby slopes the goumiers crossed on foot and by mule.

name: Point 593, Monte Cassino — the Poles take the heights
text: Point 593, the rocky summit north-west of the abbey, had defeated Americans, Indians and British since January. From 12 May General Władysław Anders' Polish II Corps attacked it and the nearby Albaneta farm, losing heavily. After the German paratroopers had been outflanked in the valley and ordered out, a patrol of the 12th Podolian Uhlan (cavalry) Regiment raised a Polish pennant over the abbey ruins on the morning of 18 May (about 10:20 by most accounts). Monte Cassino had fallen after four months.
look: Climb the short, steep path from the Polish cemetery to the white cross on Point 593 and look east: the abbey is just across the saddle, under 1 km away.

name: Pontecorvo and Aquino — the Hitler Line broken
text: Behind the Gustav Line the Germans had built a second barrier across the Liri valley, the Hitler Line (renamed Senger Line), from Piedimonte through Aquino to Pontecorvo. On 23 May the 1st Canadian Infantry Division attacked it between Pontecorvo and Aquino, at heavy cost, and broke through; the Poles took Piedimonte on 25 May. The same morning, 23 May, VI Corps began its breakout from the Anzio beachhead. Two days later the two fronts joined up.
look: Drive the minor roads between Pontecorvo and Aquino: this flat, wooded valley floor, crossed by streams, was covered by concrete tank-turret emplacements and anti-tank guns.

name: Rome — the first Axis capital to fall
text: After the breakout, Lieutenant General Mark Clark turned most of VI Corps north-west towards Rome instead of driving on to Valmontone to cut off the retreating German Tenth Army, a decision still argued over. With Hitler forbidding a defence of the city, Kesselring pulled his troops out and left Rome undefended as an open city. On 4 June 1944 American troops, including the 88th Division and the US–Canadian 1st Special Service Force, entered from the south-east; next morning Clark held a press conference on the Capitoline Hill. Two days later came D-Day.
look: Stand in Michelangelo's Piazza del Campidoglio, where Clark spoke on 5 June, and look down over the Forum: Rome was spared the destruction of so many Italian towns.

name: Lake Trasimene — the Trasimene Line
text: Two weeks after Rome fell, Kesselring's rearguards turned to fight on the Trasimene Line, a belt of hill villages running west from the lake towards Chiusi. Their aim was time: every day bought let engineers finish the Gothic Line. British 4th and 78th Divisions, the South African 6th Armoured Division and Canadian tanks fought village by village against 1st Parachute, 334th and Hermann Göring divisions until the line broke on 28 June.
look: From the lakeside walls of Castiglione del Lago look south over the low ridges towards Sanfatucchio, where the London Irish Rifles fought house to house on 21 June 1944.

name: Florence — the night of the bridges
text: As Eighth Army closed on Florence, German engineers blew every bridge over the Arno from about 22:00 on 3 August — alle Grazie, Santa Trinita, alla Carraia, San Niccolò and alla Vittoria. Only the Ponte Vecchio was spared, but the medieval streets at both ends were demolished to block it. Allied troops reached the south bank on 4 August; the partisan rising in the centre began on 11 August.
look: Stand mid-bridge and look at the rebuilt blocks along Via Por Santa Maria and Borgo San Jacopo: their plainer post-war façades mark exactly where the demolitions fell.

name: Sant'Anna di Stazzema — massacre in the Apuan hills
text: On the morning of 12 August 1944 soldiers of II Battalion, SS Panzergrenadier Regiment 35 (16th SS Division Reichsführer-SS), guided by Italian Fascist collaborators, climbed to this mountain village, which was crowded with refugees. In a few hours they killed about 560 people, sources give 540–560, among them more than 100 children (sources give 107 to 130); the youngest, Anna Pardini, was 20 days old. Ten former SS men were convicted in absentia at La Spezia in 2005; none served a sentence.
look: Walk from the church square, where many were shot and burned, up the Via Crucis path to the ossuary monument overlooking the Versilia coast.

name: Montegridolfo — the Gothic Line broken
text: Operation Olive opened on 25 August 1944 when Eighth Army, secretly shifted to the Adriatic, crossed the Metauro. By 30 August British, Canadian and Polish troops faced the main Gothic Line positions on the ridges above the Foglia. On 31 August the walled village of Montegridolfo fell to 1/4th Hampshires; Lieutenant Gerard Norton, a South African, won the Victoria Cross clearing machine-gun posts single-handed. The Line had been breached in days.
look: Walk the ramparts of this restored Malatesta hill village and look south over the Foglia valley: the attack came up those open slopes towards you.

name: Coriano Ridge — the last ridge before Rimini
text: Beyond the broken Gothic Line the Germans rushed reserves onto Coriano Ridge, the last high ground before the Romagna plain. British 1st Armoured Division's attack on 4–5 September stalled with heavy tank losses. After a bombardment by some 700 guns, the 5th Canadian and British 1st Armoured Divisions took the ridge on 12–13 September; in the week of fighting that followed towards Rimini, Eighth Army lost some 150 killed a day, according to the CWGC.
look: From the rebuilt village on the crest, face north-east: Rimini and the sea are only ten kilometres away, the prize both armies could see.

name: Il Giogo Pass — the Americans break the Apennines
text: While Eighth Army fought on the Adriatic, US Fifth Army struck the mountain Gothic Line. Instead of the heavily fortified Futa Pass on Highway 65, II Corps attacked the lesser Il Giogo Pass. For six days the 338th Infantry (85th Division) fought up Monte Altuzzo and the 363rd (91st Division) up Monticelli against the 4th Parachute Division. Both summits fell on 17–18 September at a cost of 2,731 casualties.
look: From the pass (882 m) look west to the wooded crest of Monte Altuzzo and east to Monticelli: the attackers climbed these slopes under fire from bunkers on the skyline.

name: Monte Sole — the Marzabotto massacre
text: Behind the German front south of Bologna, around 1,000 troops under SS Major Walter Reder swept the Monte Sole massif, stronghold of the Stella Rossa partisan brigade. In a week they killed about 770 people in 115 places, among them 216 children, 316 women and 142 elderly people; older counts give much higher totals. At Casaglia, villagers sheltering in the church with their priest were shot in the cemetery on 29 September.
look: Walk up to the roofless church of Casaglia and the small cemetery beside it, where the killings took place. Keep voices low; this is still a place of mourning.

name: Monte Castello — the Brazilians take their mountain
text: Monte Castello (977 m) overlooked the Brazilian sector all winter; attacks on 24–25 and 29 November and 12 December 1944 failed against the German 232nd Infantry Division. In Operation Encore the US 10th Mountain Division first scaled Riva Ridge by night on 18–19 February 1945 and stormed Monte Belvedere; then, on 21 February, the Brazilian 1st Infantry Division attacked at 06:00 and held the summit by about 17:30.
look: From the Brazilian monument on the slopes above Gaggio Montano look up the bare ridge to the summit, then west to the long wall of Riva Ridge and Monte Belvedere.

name: The Argenta Gap — the door to the Po valley
text: Operation Grapeshot opened on 9 April 1945 with a massive air and artillery bombardment on the Senio. The key was Argenta, a strip of dry land a few kilometres wide between Lake Comacchio's flooded marshes and the Reno. British V Corps forced it with commandos, amphibious Fantails and Kangaroo armoured carriers against the 42nd Jäger and 29th Panzergrenadier Divisions. Argenta fell on 18 April and British armour broke out towards the Po.
look: Look round the flat reclaimed land outside Argenta: canals, embankments and the Reno levees were the only cover, and the floods on either side made them lethal funnels.

name: Bologna liberated
text: After six months of stalemate within sight of the city, the German front south of Bologna collapsed on 20 April 1945. Early on 21 April troops of the Polish II Corps and the US 34th Division entered from east and south, joined by the Italian Legnano Combat Group and partisans. On the wall of Palazzo d'Accursio, where partisans had been executed, families began pinning photographs of their dead that same day.
look: In Piazza del Nettuno study the wall of ceramic tiles bearing the names and faces of more than 2,000 fallen partisans, beside the Salaborsa library.

name: San Benedetto Po — first across the Po
text: Breaking onto the plain, US IV Corps raced north. Spearheads of the 10th Mountain Division reached the Po at San Benedetto at 18:00 on 22 April and crossed in assault boats on 23 April without losing a man. Downstream the 88th Division, British and South Africans followed, trapping thousands of Germans south of the river; the bridges were gone and heavy weapons were abandoned on the banks.
look: Climb the Po embankment near the abbey town and look across the wide brown river: this is what the retreating German armies had to cross with no bridges left.

name: Giulino di Mezzegra — the end of Mussolini
text: On 25 April 1945 the partisan committee called the general insurrection; Genoa, Milan and Turin rose as the Germans pulled out. Mussolini, fleeing towards Switzerland with a German column, was caught at Dongo on 27 April and, by the official account, shot with Clara Petacci outside Villa Belmonte here the next afternoon; details remain disputed. On 29 April the surrender of German forces in Italy was signed at Caserta, effective 2 May.
look: A memorial at the gate of Villa Belmonte marks the traditional spot. This is a quiet residential lane between private houses: be brief and respectful.
